source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Measured Moves Based on the Size of the First Leg (the Spike)

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: SpikePauseBarPrimitive
candidates.quote: The next bar was a small doji bar, and this pause meant that the spike ended on the prior bar, which was the last of the consecutive bull trend bars... That doji was the first bar that lacked momentum and it therefore told you that the spike had ended on the previous bar.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: a spike (run of consecutive same-direction trend bars) is deemed to have ended at the bar before the first 'pause' bar - a doji, a bar with a large opposite-side tail, or a bar with an opposite-color body.
candidates.pseudocode: isPauseBar[0] = DojiBar[0] || close[0] < open[0] || (high[0]-max(open[0],close[0])) >= largeTailFraction*(high[0]-low[0]); spikeEndIndex = firstPauseBarIndexSinceSpikeStart - 1
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (state marker for where the spike's height should be measured)

complexity.reason: forward scan from a detected spike start until the first bar that breaks momentum

notes: Feeds every measured-move target below that is anchored to 'the spike'.

candidates.name: SpikeOpenToCloseMeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: The open of the first bar was eight points below the close of the third and final bull trend bar in the spike, so the spike should be thought of as being eight points tall, at a minimum... take the number of points from the open of the first bar of the spike to the close of the final bar of the spike and add that to the close of that final bar of the spike.
candidates.description: Primary measured-move formula: spikeHeight = close[lastSpikeBar] - open[firstSpikeBar]; target = close[lastSpikeBar] + spikeHeight; take profit on the long when price reaches it.
candidates.pseudocode: spikeHeight = close[lastSpikeBar] - open[firstSpikeBar]; target = close[lastSpikeBar] + spikeHeight; high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: the spike's start/end bars must persist once identified; the arithmetic itself is trivial

notes: Distinct from R08-22's SpikeHeightMeasuredMove, which used high[end]-low[start]; this chapter's primary reference points are open-of-first to close-of-last. Dedup pass should compare/merge the family.

candidates.name: SpikeAlternateMeasurementVariants
candidates.quote: You could use the low of the first bar to the high of the third bar or even the high of the doji fourth bar, but it is more conservative to use the smaller figure for your initial projection. If the second leg surpasses this target, then look at other targets.
candidates.description: Compute the alternate spike-height references (low-of-first-bar to high-of-last-bar; open-of-first to high-of-last; including the pause bar) as additional, usually larger, candidate targets; check the smallest (most conservative) target first and escalate to the next larger one only once the market surpasses it.
candidates.pseudocode: targets = sort_ascending([openToCloseTarget, lowToHighTarget, openToHighTarget]); currentTarget = firstTargetNotYetSurpassed(targets); high[0] >= currentTarget - toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: profit-taking limit, escalating through successive projections

complexity.reason: builds on the already-identified spike endpoints; only the multi-target escalation logic is new

candidates.name: ProtectiveStopBeyondSpikeStart
candidates.quote: the initial protective stop is usually beyond the beginning of the first move. For example, if there is a strong buy spike, then the initial protective stop is one tick below the low of the spike.
candidates.description: Exit the long if price trades below the low of the identified spike's start (a wider, spike-anchored alternative to a signal-bar or entry-bar stop).
candidates.book_order_type: protective sell stop beyond the start of the spike

complexity.reason: needs the spike's start bar remembered from R07-01

notes: Distinct from R05-14 (stop below the entry bar): here the reference is the spike's own start, which may be several bars before the entry.

candidates.name: ChannelHeightEqualsSpikeHeightTarget
candidates.quote: There is a variation of this in spike and channel trends where the height of the channel is often about the same as the height of the spike. This is especially true when the spike is strong... The channel that follows usually will find some resistance in that area and the market will often then correct down to the bottom of the channel.
candidates.description: After a spike ends and a channel begins, expect the channel's own height to approximate the spike's height; once price extends spikeHeight beyond the end of the spike (within the channel), treat that as resistance/a profit-taking area.
candidates.pseudocode: target = spikeEndPrice + spikeHeight; high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: arithmetically identical to R07-02's target; the only new content is the channel-height framing

notes: Numerically the same target as R07-02 when measured from the spike's end; kept separate because the book frames it as a channel property, not a spike property, and pairs it with R07-06's channel-bottom correction target.

candidates.name: ChannelBottomRetestAfterMeasuredMove
candidates.quote: The market invariably overshoots and has to backtrack to home in on a 50-50 market. The measured move area is an overshoot of the odds, and they then briefly favor the bears. Once the market retraces to the bottom of the channel, the odds again overshoot, but this time in favor of the bulls.
candidates.description: After price reaches the spike/channel measured-move target (R07-05) and reverses, project the correction's target at the bottom of the channel that followed the spike; this is both a place to expect support and a re-entry area for the trend.
candidates.pseudocode: channelBottom = lowest(low, channelBars); low[0] <= channelBottom + toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: buy near the bottom of the channel (re-entry) or cover a countertrend short there

complexity.reason: needs a remembered channel-bottom level in addition to the already-tracked measured-move target

candidates.name: Leg1EqualsLeg2MeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: When a market makes a sharp move and then has a pullback, it will likely have a second leg and the second leg is frequently approximately the same size as the first. This is a leg 1 = leg 2 move, but it is also called an ABC move or an AB = CD... for the AB = CD in a bull trend, if you start at point A and add the length of the AB leg (which is B - A), then add that to C, you get C + (B - A).
candidates.description: The classic leg-1-equals-leg-2 (AB=CD) measured move: given swing points A (leg 1 start), B (leg 1 end), C (pullback end/leg 2 start), target D = C + (B - A); take profit on the long when price reaches D.
candidates.pseudocode: A = mostRecentSwingLow(pivotStrength, lookback)[2]; B = mostRecentSwingHigh(pivotStrength, lookback)[1]; C = mostRecentSwingLow(pivotStrength, lookback); target = C + (B - A); high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: profit-taking limit at the projection; countertrend setups may also be considered near it

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection for three points (A, B, C), the canonical measured-move construction this chapter is named for

notes: Brooks explicitly rejects the confusing ABCD/AB=CD alphabetical labeling in favor of 'leg 1 / pullback / leg 2'; kept here under the simpler name.

Mathematically identical to computing the target from the pullback's midpoint (the 'thick area' argument, p71-72): C + (B-A) = thickAreaMid + (thickAreaMid - A) when C is the pullback's low and thickAreaMid = (B+C)/2 is not generally equal, but the book shows both formulas resolve to C + (B-A); the thick-area version is not separately encoded since it is the same target.

candidates.name: NestedLegMeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: a trader could look at AD as a first leg that contains two smaller legs (AB and CD), and then stay long until there was a measured move up (AD = EF, and the target is the top of the solid line).
candidates.description: Apply the leg-1-equals-leg-2 construction one level up: treat an entire two-legged move (A to D, itself made of smaller legs AB and CD) as the new 'leg 1', and project an equal move E-to-F after the next pullback (E).
candidates.pseudocode: legHeight = D - A; target = E + legHeight; high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: profit-taking limit at the larger-scale projection

complexity.reason: same swing-pivot dependency as R07-07 but one scale up, requiring a hierarchy of pivots (A,B,C,D,E)

candidates.name: TradingRangeMidpointMeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: When a market has a strong trend move and then a fairly strong pullback leg, and then a trading range, traders can use the approximate middle of the range to project where the second leg of the pullback might reach. As the trading range unfolds, keep adjusting the line to where you estimate the midpoint is, and that will usually be around the midpoint of the pullback once the move has finally completed its second leg.
candidates.description: While a pullback trading range is still developing, continuously project target = 2 x rangeMidpoint - pullbackStart, updating rangeMidpoint each bar as the range's own highest-high/lowest-low midpoint (equivalent to a leg-1=leg-2 measured move using a moving estimate of point C).
candidates.pseudocode: rangeMidpoint = (highest(high, rangeBars) + lowest(low, rangeBars)) / 2; target = 2 * rangeMidpoint - pullbackStart; high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: profit-taking limit at the projection, continuously re-estimated

complexity.reason: the target is recomputed every bar from a rolling window rather than fixed once at a detected pivot

candidates.name: AmbiguousLegStartMultipleTargetsFilter
candidates.quote: astute traders were open to the possibility that the correction up to bar 9 began at bar 4 and not bar 6, and therefore thought that the second leg down might be equal to the bar 1 to bar 4 first leg down instead of the bar 1 to bar 6 first leg down.
candidates.description: When the true start of leg 1 is ambiguous among multiple plausible swing points, compute a leg-1=leg-2 target from each candidate start and watch all of them, rather than committing to a single measured move.
candidates.pseudocode: targets = [C + (B - candidateA_i) for candidateA_i in plausibleLegStarts]; for each target, test high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks*tickSize

complexity.reason: choosing which swing points are 'plausible' candidate leg starts is itself a design decision, not a mechanical test

notes: Figure 7.2's worked example; the book also raises an Elliott Wave 'flat' interpretation for this ambiguity, which is not itself mechanizable (see rejected).

candidates.name: TradingRangeExtremeFavorsReversionFilter
candidates.quote: when the market is at the bottom of a trading range, the probability favors a move up; and when it is at the top of the range, the probability favors a move down. This is because of market inertia... about 80 percent of attempts to break out of a trading range fail
candidates.description: Filter: inside an identified trading range, favor long entries near the range's low and short entries near the range's high (fade the extremes) over betting on a breakout.
candidates.pseudocode: isTradingRange && close[0] <= rangeLow + nearExtremeFraction * (rangeHigh - rangeLow) => favorLongFade; close[0] >= rangeHigh - nearExtremeFraction * (rangeHigh - rangeLow) => favorShortFade
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter favoring fade entries over breakout entries)

complexity.reason: 'trading range' identification is a design decision; the fade-the-extremes logic itself is simple once the range boundaries exist

notes: Restates the 'inertia' idea already used in R05-08/RP2-07; this instance emphasizes the specific 80% breakout-failure figure Brooks gives for trading ranges.

candidates.name: OpenMiddleRangeCloseNearOpenTarget
candidates.quote: Whenever a day has an average range and the open is in the middle of the range, the market often tries to close around the open.
candidates.description: On a session whose developing range is close to its recent average and whose open sits near the middle of that range, treat the session open as a late-day magnet/target for the close.
candidates.pseudocode: todaysRange = highest(high, barsToday) - lowest(low, barsToday); abs(todaysRange - avgDailyRange(adrLookback)) <= rangeTolFrac * avgDailyRange(adrLookback) && abs(sessionOpen - (highest(high, barsToday) + lowest(low, barsToday)) / 2) <= midToleranceTicks * tickSize => targetLevel = sessionOpen
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (late-session target for a fade back toward the open)

complexity.reason: 'average range' and 'middle of the range' are fuzzy comparisons needing a design decision on tolerance

notes: Daily-chart example (Figure 7.2's first day) shown as an almost-perfect doji candle from this effect.

rejected.quote: at bar 1 the market was surprised by an announcement about the president proposing new banking regulations, and this led to two large bear trend bars
rejected.reason: news event; the resulting spike/measured-move behavior is already captured generically in R07-01..R07-04 without the news cause

rejected.quote: Fibonacci traders also look to other extensions (138 percent, 150 percent, 162 percent, etc.) as valid areas in which to look for reversals, but this is too complicated and approximate.
rejected.reason: Brooks explicitly dismisses this as too complicated/approximate and gives no concrete rule beyond the ratios already covered by RP2-03

rejected.quote: Elliott Wave traders know that upward corrections can include a pullback that goes below the bottom of the initial move down, and they call this sideways type of correction a flat.
rejected.reason: Elliott Wave pattern labeling is discretionary interpretation with no stated bar-level test

chapter_summary: The book's core measured-move chapter: formalizes the spike-height projection (open-of-first-bar to close-of-last-bar of a spike, plus alternate low/high references, checked smallest-first) and the classic leg-1-equals-leg-2 / AB=CD construction, including a nested (nested-leg) nested-hierarchy variant and a continuously-updated trading-range-midpoint variant. All are Exit targets; the leg-based ones are graded hard because they need swing-pivot detection, while the spike-based ones are moderate because the spike's own endpoints (via the shared SpikePauseBarPrimitive) are enough to anchor them without full pivot machinery. A stop-placement rule anchors the protective stop to the spike's start rather than the entry or signal bar. Two Entry-side context filters (trading-range-extreme reversion, ambiguous-leg-start multiple targets) and one intraday curiosity (open-in-the-middle-of-an-average-range days tend to close near the open) round out the chapter. Much of the chapter's prose is a probability/mathematics discussion (50-50 markets, 60-80 percent figures) justifying why measured moves work; that reasoning itself produced no new bar-level candidates beyond what is listed, and the worked examples (Figures 7.1-7.5) are applications of R07-01, R07-02, and R07-07/08 rather than new rule types. Dedup pass should compare this family closely against Chapter 8's gap-based measured moves (R08-05, R08-09, R08-10, R08-12, R08-13, R08-22) and Chapter 5's wedge/spike targets (R05-19, R05-20) - all are variations on 'project a completed leg's height from a new reference point.'
